Supreme Court: Second Amendment Protects all Bearable Arms!

No, that's what Samuel Alito said. That's NOT the opinion of the court. The court sent the case BACK to the lower court to rule again. That lower court could still find another reason to rule stun guns illegal, and the Supreme Sourt could uphold that new decision. This article is misleading, just like your headline.

This has article has nothing to do with tasers. Who cares about tasers. What Alito did was slip in an opinion relating to "all bearable arms" being protected under the Second Amendment regardless if they were invented yet when the Constitution was written. Further, he raises the bar on what is considered "unusual or dangerous" which strengthens the Heller ruling and puts a big question mark on the Firearms Owner Protection Act of 1986. This isn't as strong as a ruling of the court and all of its members but will absolutely be used as precedent next time a state tries to pass an "assault weapon" ban or a "high capacity magazine" ban.

Maybe. Or maybe Massachusetts will come up with different reasoning, and SCOTUS will agree, saying that the second amendment isn't absolute, and you can still ban arms that meet xzy conditions. We know Alito's opinion, but remember that Heller v. DC was 5-4, and if Scalia's replacement is anti-gun, the court will support loads of restriction as constitutional, provided they are worded correctly. Last year SCOTUS refused to hear an extremely important carry case, which could signify a lot of things, many of them bad for 2A rights. The ruling in the article isn't a loss for 2A rights, but it's not a huge win either, and it definitely is not a clear ruling saying that the 2A PROTECTS ALL BEARABLE ARMS like the headline says.
So wait, what does this actually mean? Obama stops trying to ban gun? Or States cannot outlaw guns?

It means that states can't ban arms for the following reasons: 1. because they didn't exist when the constitution was written (the "2A only protect muskets" bullshit - this may have already been part of the Heller decision anyway) 2. because they are not useful for military purposes

It also means that you can't say a gun is "dangerous and unusual" because it didn't exist in 1776. Theoretically, states can still ban guns for being dangerous and unusual under Heller, but they have to give another reason why they think they meet those conditions.

Since the court did not find any problems with the defendant carrying her weapon outside the home, and using it for self-defense, some people think it's the same thing as the court saying "You can carry weapons outside the home for self defense." But they never said that. The question still has not been settled completely. Nor has the question of what exactly constitutes "dangerous and unusual."

What SCOTUS actually did was vacate the lower court's decision - basically giving them a "do over." They didn't overturn the lower court's decision, and make a final ruling. Now, Massachusetts can overturn the woman's conviction, or they can affirm it, like they did before, but use different reasoning as to why it was OK to ban certain arms. If they affirm her conviction again, it will get appealed again, and SCOTUS will either let it stand, overturn it, or vacate it again.

That's most of it.
